entry: Organism that lives or thrives in extreme environments, such as very hot or cold conditions, high pressure, high radiation, high salinity or extreme pH. Extremophiles are mainly [[Microorganism|microorganisms]], chiefly [[Bacteria|bacteria]] and archaea, though some eukaryotes, such as certain fungi and [[Tardigrade|tardigrades]], also qualify. Because an extreme environment is defined relative to an anthropocentric standard, these organisms are considered ecologically dominant in the planet's evolutionary history. Bacteria have been found living in a lake buried a half-mile deep under ice in [[Antarctica]] and in the [[Mariana Trench]]. Studies of extremophiles have expanded knowledge of the limits of life and inform speculation about [[Extraterrestrial life|extraterrestrial life]].

Manufacturing process of pushing material through a die to form objects with a fixed cross-sectional profile. Its advantages include the ability to create very complex cross-sections, to work brittle materials, which encounter only compressive and shear stresses, and to produce an excellent surface finish. Drawing, which pulls material through a die using tensile strength, is the main way to produce [[Wire|wire]]. Commonly extruded materials include [[Metal|metals]], [[Polymer|polymers]], [[Ceramic|ceramics]] and [[Concrete]]. Joseph Bramah patented the first extrusion process, for pipe made from soft metals, in 1797. Harder materials such as [[Steel|steel]] began to be extruded in 1951, and extrusion can also increase the strength of metals.

American multinational oil and gas company, headquartered in Spring, Texas, near [[Houston]]. Formed in 1999 by the merger of Exxon and Mobil, it is the largest direct successor of [[John D. Rockefeller]]'s [[Standard Oil]]. It is vertically integrated across the oil and gas industry and is the largest investor-owned oil company in the world. The 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill in [[Alaska]] is considered one of the worst in terms of environmental damage, and the company has faced criticism and lawsuits over environmental incidents and its past positions on [[Climate change|climate change]].

Polygenic phenotypic trait determined by the pigmentation of the iris and the scattering of light in the iris stroma. In humans, iris pigmentation ranges from light brown to black, depending on the concentration of [[Melanin|melanin]]. Blue, green and hazel eyes result from light scattering in the stroma, a process similar to [[Rayleigh scattering]] that makes the sky blue; neither blue nor green pigments are present in the human iris. As of 2010, as many as 16 [[Gene|genes]] had been associated with human eye color, the main two being OCA2 and HERC2.

Series of tests performed to assess vision, focusing ability and other functions of the eyes, usually by an optometrist, ophthalmologist or orthoptist. A full examination begins with a medical history and includes eight steps: visual acuity, pupil function, extraocular muscle motility, intraocular pressure, visual fields, external examination, slit-lamp examination and dilated fundoscopic examination. [[Refraction]] testing assesses how light bends through the eye to identify the need for corrective lenses. Examinations can detect treatable blinding diseases and eye signs of systemic conditions such as [[Diabetes|diabetes]] and [[Hypertension|hypertension]]. Corticosteroids can raise intraocular pressure, which can lead to [[Glaucoma|glaucoma]].

American journalist and political commentator. Klein co-founded the explanatory news website Vox in 2014 and in November 2020 joined [[The New York Times]] as a columnist. He managed Wonkblog at [[The Washington Post]] and hosts The Ezra Klein Show, a [[Podcast|podcast]]. His books include *Why We're Polarized* (January 2020).

American poet and critic, a major figure in early modernist poetry and a collaborator in [[Fascism|Fascist]] Italy during [[World War II]]. Pound helped develop Imagism, a movement stressing precision and economy of language. As foreign editor of several American literary magazines in London, he helped shape the work of [[Ernest Hemingway]], [[T. S. Eliot]] and [[James Joyce]], including the serialization of *Ulysses*. He moved to Italy in 1924, embraced [[Benito Mussolini]]'s fascism and expressed support for [[Adolf Hitler]]. During World War II he recorded hundreds of paid radio broadcasts for the fascist Italian government. Indicted for treason by the United States in 1945, he was ruled unfit for trial and spent over 12 years at St. Elizabeths Hospital in Washington, D.C. His economic and political views have kept his legacy highly controversial.

Jewish scribe and priest, the main character of the *Book of Ezra* in the [[Hebrew Bible]]. According to the Bible, he was an important scribe (*sofer*) and priest (*kohen*) in the early Second Temple period. Sent by the Achaemenid emperor Artaxerxes I from [[Babylon]] to [[Jerusalem]], he led a group of exiles, reintroduced the [[Torah]] and enforced the dissolution of marriages with foreign women. He is highly respected in Judaism and is venerated as a saint by the [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic Church]] and the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]]. Historians have no consensus on his historicity or mission, owing to a lack of extrabiblical evidence.

Association football club based in [[Barcelona]], [[Catalonia]], Spain. Founded in 1899 and owned and operated by its supporters, the club competes in [[La Liga]] and is a symbol of Catalan culture, with the motto *Més que un club* ("More than a club"). It has won 22 European and worldwide titles, including five [[UEFA Champions League]] titles, and has won a record 82 domestic trophies. Barcelona players have won a joint record 12 Ballon d'Or awards, with recipients including [[Johan Cruyff]].

Professional sports club based in [[Munich]], [[Bavaria]], Germany, best known for its men's football team in the [[Bundesliga]]. Founded in 1900 by eleven players, Bayern is the most successful club in German football, with a record 35 national titles and a record 21 national cups, the DFB-Pokal. It has won six [[UEFA Champions League]] titles, a German record, and won the European Cup three consecutive times from 1974 to 1976 under the captaincy of [[Franz Beckenbauer]].

International [[Association football|association football]] competition for women's national teams, held every four years since 1991. The United States has won four of the nine tournaments, with [[Germany]] winning two and Japan, Norway and Spain one each. Eight countries have hosted the tournament, including [[Canada]] and [[France]]. The 2031 edition is expected to be co-hosted by Costa Rica, Jamaica, Mexico and the United States, and will be the first to feature 48 teams.

International [[Association football|association football]] competition among the senior men's national teams of [[FIFA]] members, held every four years since 1930. It was not held in 1942 or 1946 because of [[World War II]]. The 2026 tournament, with 48 teams, was won by Spain, which defeated the holders, Argentina. [[Brazil]] has won five titles, the most of any nation, followed by Germany and Italy with four each, Argentina with three, and France, Spain and Uruguay with two each. The 2018 tournament's viewership was estimated at 3.57 billion, close to half the global population.

International governing body of [[Association football|association football]], beach soccer and futsal, founded in 1904 in [[Paris]] and headquartered in [[Zurich]]. Its 211 member associations belong to six confederations, including UEFA in [[Europe]] and CAF in [[Africa]]. FIFA organizes the [[FIFA World Cup|World Cup]], and its tournaments generate revenue from sponsorships. In 2015 the U.S. Department of Justice indicted nine officials and executives on racketeering, wire fraud and bribery charges.

American actor, best known for his portrayal of Antonio Salieri in the film *Amadeus* (1984). He won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Actor for that role. Raised in [[El Paso, Texas|El Paso]], he made his Broadway debut in 1968 and received an Obie Award for his roles in [[Anton Chekhov]]'s *Uncle Vanya* and [[William Shakespeare]]'s *The Merchant of Venice*. His films include *Scarface* and *The Grand Budapest Hotel*, and he was a regular on the television series *Homeland*.

American novelist and short-story writer whose works depict the excess of the Jazz Age. Raised mainly in New York, he attended [[Princeton University]] before leaving to join the Army during [[World War I]]; while stationed in [[Alabama]] he met Zelda Sayre, whom he later married. *This Side of Paradise* (1920) made him famous, and *The Great Gatsby* (1925) is hailed by some critics as the "Great American Novel" despite weak early sales. He was part of the [[Lost Generation]] expatriate circle in Europe, including [[Ernest Hemingway]]. He struggled with [[Alcoholism|alcoholism]] in the 1920s and with money during the [[Great Depression]]. *Tender Is the Night* (1934) was completed after his wife's placement in a mental institution for [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]].

German film director, producer and screenwriter, regarded as one of the most influential filmmakers of the silent era. His *Nosferatu* (1922), an unauthorized adaptation of [[Bram Stoker]]'s novel *Dracula*, is considered a masterpiece of German Expressionist cinema, although copyright issues limited its commercial success. He immigrated to Hollywood in 1926 and made *Sunrise* (1927), which critics regard as among the best films ever made. He travelled to [[Bora Bora]] to make *Tabu* (1931) with documentary pioneer Robert J. Flaherty, but disputes led him to complete the film alone. Of the 21 films he directed, eight are considered completely lost.

Ivorian politician and physician, first president of [[Ivory Coast]] (1960–1993). Economic growth based on sound planning, strong ties with France and the coffee and cocoa industries became known as the "Ivorian miracle". He moved the capital from [[Abidjan]] to his hometown of Yamoussoukro and built the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace there at a cost of US$300 million. He aided the conspirators who ousted [[Kwame Nkrumah]] from power in [[Ghana]] in 1966. Critics argue that his one-party state suppressed political pluralism and that his administration faced allegations of corruption. At the time of his death he was the longest-serving leader in Africa's history. In 1989, [[UNESCO]] created a peace prize named for him.

Front or exterior of a [[Building|building]], often its most important aspect in [[Architecture|architectural]] design. The word, a loanword from French meaning "frontage" or "face", has its earliest recorded usage in English in 1656, according to the [[Oxford English Dictionary]]. Façades affect energy efficiency, and historic façades are often restricted by local [[Zoning|zoning]] regulations. High-rise façades are commonly made of aluminum or [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]], and [[Titanium|titanium]] has been used in recent years despite its cost. Outside architecture, "façade" describes a deceptive outward appearance.

Large family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], also called the [[Legume|legume]], pea or bean family, with nearly 20,000 known species. It is the third-largest land plant family by number of species, behind Orchidaceae and [[Asteraceae]]. Its members range from giant trees to small herbs, and it is the most common family in tropical rainforests and dry forests of the Americas and Africa. Crops include [[Soybean|soybean]] and [[Peanut|peanut]], and legumes have been staple foods for millennia. Many species host nitrogen-fixing [[Bacteria|bacteria]] in root nodules, which reduces the need for synthetic fertilizers.

Short fictional story in prose or verse that illustrates a moral lesson through animals, plants or objects that speak and act like humans. Fables differ from parables in using such non-human actors. The best-known Western fables are attributed to the legendary [[Aesop's Fables|Aesop]], supposed to have been a slave in [[Ancient Greece]] around 550 BCE. In the first century AD, Phaedrus produced [[Latin]] verse versions that were transmitted through the [[Middle Ages]]. In [[India]], the [[Panchatantra]] sets beast fables inside a frame of instruction in practical conduct. Anansi stories originate with the tribes of [[Ghana]], and [[George Orwell]]'s *Animal Farm* uses the form for political satire.

Front part of the head of a [[Human|human]] or other [[Mammal|mammal]], featuring the eyes, nose and mouth. Mammals have evolved diverse facial forms, especially among [[Primate|primates]], whose forward-facing eyes allow binocular vision and depth perception. The human chin is unique to *Homo sapiens*, distinguishing modern humans from [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]]. Facial muscles allow humans to express [[Emotion|emotions]], and the face is the feature that best distinguishes an individual. Facial shape, influenced by the skull, is an important determinant of [[Beauty|beauty]], including facial symmetry. Surface differences such as [[Eye color|eye color]] may also contribute to racist ideologies and discrimination.

American [[Social networking service|social networking service]] owned by Meta Platforms. Founded in 2004 by [[Mark Zuckerberg]] and fellow [[Harvard University|Harvard]] students, it was initially limited to Harvard before expanding to other universities. It was the most downloaded mobile application of the 2010s, and as of December 2023 it reported approximately 3.07 billion monthly active users. Users can create profiles and share text, photos and video, and access the service from [[Smartphone|smartphones]] and personal computers. The service has been criticized over user privacy, including the Cambridge Analytica data scandal, political manipulation, addiction and [[Self-esteem|low self-esteem]], and content such as fake news and hate speech.

True datum about one or more aspects of a circumstance or occurrence in the real world. The word derives from Latin *factum*, meaning "a thing done". Scientific facts are verified by careful, repeatable observation or measurement, including [[Experiment|experiments]]. In [[Philosophy|philosophy]], a fact is the worldly correlate of a true proposition, a state of affairs that makes the proposition true. Facts are considered in [[Epistemology|epistemology]] and possibly [[Ontology|ontology]]. In 1870, [[Charles Sanders Peirce]] described four ways people fix belief: tenacity, authority, a priori reasoning and the [[Scientific method|scientific method]].

Product of all positive [[Integer|integers]] less than or equal to a non-negative integer *n*, written *n*!. For example, 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120, and by convention 0! = 1. In [[Combinatorics|combinatorics]], *n*! counts the [[Permutation|permutations]] of *n* distinct objects. Factorials appear in the power series of the [[Exponential function|exponential function]], and [[Stirling's approximation|Stirling's approximation]] approximates them accurately for large numbers. [[Leonhard Euler]] and Daniel Bernoulli extended the factorial to complex numbers, except at negative integers, through the [[Gamma function|gamma function]]. The concept arose independently in several ancient cultures, including Jain literature and the Hebrew mystical text *Sefer Yetzirah*.

Industrial facility, often a complex of buildings filled with machinery, where workers make or process [[Goods|goods]]. Factories arose during the [[Industrial Revolution]], when capital and space requirements outgrew cottage industry and workshops. Most modern factories are warehouse-like buildings with heavy equipment for [[Assembly line|assembly line]] production, often located with access to rail, [[Highway|highway]] and water transport. Continuous-production industries, such as chemicals, pulp and paper, and refined oil, use heat or [[Electricity|electricity]] to transform streams of raw materials into finished products. The term mill originates with grain milling, which was powered by water or wind until steam replaced it in the 19th century. [[Max Weber]] did not regard ancient or medieval production as factory production.
